claim: CD40 signaling in B cells via the non-canonical NFκB pathway invokes nuclear translocation of heterodimeric RelB/p52.
source: CD40 signals via the non-canonical NFκB pathway that uniquely invokes the nuclear translocation of heterodimeric RelB/p52 (Fusco et al., 2008; Hömig-Hölzel et al., 2008; Vallabhapurapu and Karin, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies (Fusco et al., 2008; Hömig-Hölzel et al., 2008; Vallabhapurapu and Karin, 2009).

claim: Nuclear RelB was observed in a subset of transferred NP-specific B cells by day 2 and 3 post-immunization.
source: As expected, nuclear RelB was observed in a subset of transferred NP-specific B cells by IF histology day 2 and 3 p.i. (p.i.) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence histology data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: Blocking CD40 interactions resulted in the loss of RelB expression in responding B cells.
source: As blocking CD40 interactions resulted in the loss of RelB expression in responding B cells, we found elevated RelB to be a reliable indicator of CD40 signaling and used it as surrogate marker for recent signaling events (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing loss of RelB upon CD40 blockade, presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two days post-immunization, GFP+ NP-specific B cells were found predominantly in the interfollicular zone and at the T/B border and were RelB+ and IRF4+, but expressed undetectable levels of BCL6.
source: Two days p.i., GFP+ NP-specific B cells were found predominantly in the IF zone and at the T / B border and were RelB+ and IRF4+, but expressed undetectable levels of BCL6 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence histology data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BCL6 expression was not apparent among NP-specific B cells until day 3 post-immunization.
source: Consistent with our prior study, expression of BCL6 was not apparent among NP-specific B cells until d3 p.i., a point in time when they remained largely constrained to the IF zone (Kerfoot et al., 2011) (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1B and is consistent with a prior published study (Kerfoot et al., 2011).

claim: All BCL6 expressing B cells at day 3 post-immunization harbored nuclear RelB and IRF4.
source: Strikingly, we found that all BCL6 expressing B cells at this time point harbored nuclear RelB and IRF4, although the BCL6 expression levels of such cells was less than observed in fully differentiated GC B cells (Figure 1B and data not shown; discrimination of nuclear RelB from the cytoplasmic form is demonstrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: By day 3.5 post-immunization, GFP+ B cells expressing higher levels of BCL6 with diminished levels of RelB and IRF4 began to emerge.
source: Only a half day later (d3.5), GFP+ B cells expressing higher levels of BCL6 with diminished levels of RelB and IRF4 began to emerge (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: BCL6hi RelB- cells were located much deeper within follicles, whereas BCL6int RelB+ cells resided mainly outside of follicles or close to follicular borders.
source: Image analysis comparing BCL6+ RelB+ cells to BCL6+ RelB- cells revealed that the newly formed BCL6hi RelB- cells were located much deeper within follicles, whereas BCL6int RelB+ cells resided mainly outside of follicles or close to follicular borders (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by image analysis data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The expression of RelB in BCL6int IRF4+ cells is significantly higher than in BCL6hi IRF4lo GC B cells.
source: Consistent with the histology data, the expression of RelB in BCL6int IRF4+ cells is significantly higher in BCL6hi IRF4lo GC B cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The BCL6int population emerged by 3 days post-immunization, before the appearance of intrafollicular GC B cells, peaked at day 3.5 and rapidly declined by day 8 when GC B cells were abundant.
source: The BCL6int population evidenced an early and transient pattern: it emerged by 3 days pi., before the appearance of intrafollicular GC B cells, peaked at day 3.5 and rapidly declined by day 8 when GC B cells were abundant (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing temporal dynamics in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: BCL6int RelB+ IRF4+ nascent GC B cell precursors expressed lower levels of PNA binding and Fas compared to their BCL6hi GC B cell counterparts.
source: They expressed lower levels of PNA binding and Fas and less repression of the BCL6 target gene CD38 compared to their BCL6hi GC B cell counterparts (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Significantly higher levels of CD86 were observed among the BCL6int RelB+ IRF4+ GC precursors.
source: Interestingly, significantly higher levels of CD86 were observed among the BCL6int RelB+ IRF4+ GC precursors.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The majority of antigen specific B cells underwent six rounds of division 3 days post-immunization, and two or more additional divisions over the following day.
source: We found that the majority of antigen specific B cells underwent six rounds of division 3 days p.i., and two or more additional divisions over the following day (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Most GC precursors were found to have undergone 4–6 divisions.
source: With these immunization conditions, most GC precursors were found to have undergone 4–6 divisions (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: GC precursors were significantly less frequent among cells that have undergone seven or more divisions, coincident with the emergence of GC B cells at divisions 6–7.
source: In contrast, GC precursors were significantly less frequent among cells that have undergone seven or more divisions, coincident with the emergence of GC B cells at divisions 6–7 (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: GC precursors were predominantly in cell cycle and not evidently apoptotic compared to non-responding B cells.
source: Cell cycle analysis indicated that GC precursors were predominantly in cell cycle and not evidently apoptotic compared to non-responding B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell cycle and apoptosis analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: A gradual reduction of RelB through rounds of cell divisions was observed in GC precursors.
source: In contrast to relatively stable expression of BCL6 and IRF4, a gradual reduction of RelB through rounds of cell divisions was observed (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing RelB levels across cell divisions in Figure 4D.

claim: A low dose of NP-CGG resulted in a smaller percentage of GC precursors but a significantly larger percentage of GC B cells.
source: A low dose of NP-CGG resulted in a smaller percentage of GC precursors but a significantly larger percentage of GC B cells (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data comparing different antigen doses shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: With the lower dose of NP-CGG, GC B cells emerged at divisions 4–6.
source: With the lower dose of NP-CGG, GC B cells emerged at divisions 4–6, suggesting that GC precursors are predisposed to differentiate with fewer rounds of divisions when mice received lower doses of Ag (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: The introduction of either NP-CGG or anti-CD40 at day 3 markedly impeded the GC B cell transition but significantly increased the frequency of their immediate precursors.
source: Interestingly, the introduction of either NP-CGG or anti-CD40 at day 3 markedly impeded the GC B cell transition but significantly increased the frequency of their immediate precursors (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: IRF4 levels were elevated in GC precursors when either additional antigen or agonistic anti-CD40 was introduced compared to treatment controls.
source: Although overall RelB levels were not affected, IRF4 levels were elevated in GC precursors compared to treatment controls (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: GC precursors did not display the typical pattern of RelB reduction at later cell divisions when either additional antigen or agonistic anti-CD40 is introduced.
source: Further examination of CFSE-labeled B cells revealed that GC precursors did not display the typical pattern of RelB reduction at later cell divisions when either additional antigen or agonistic anti-CD40 is introduced (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFSE dilution and RelB expression data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Both treatments (additional antigen or anti-CD40) strongly promoted the formation of plasmablasts.
source: In sharp contrast, both treatments strongly promoted the formation of plasmablasts (Figure 6I,J).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing plasmablast formation in Figure 6I and 6J.

claim: Both CD4+ T cell depletion and CD40L blockade resulted in a rapid reduction in detectable GC precursors just a half day later, while GC B cell frequencies remained comparable.
source: Although both treatments resulted in a rapid reduction in detectable GC precursors just a half day later, GC B cell frequencies remained comparable (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7B, 7C, and 7D.

claim: Short-term blockade of CD40L did not lead to an increase in apoptosis of GC precursors.
source: This short-term blockade of CD40L did not lead to an increase in apoptosis of GC precursors (Figure 7E–F) or cell cycle arrest (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by apoptosis analysis data shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: The majority of RelB+ BCL6+ B cells (64%) were in direct contact with OVA-specific T cells, while few RelBlo BCL6+ B cells were in contact with cognate T cells (17%).
source: Whereas the majority of RelB+ BCL6+ B cells (64%, n = 86 from tissue sections of 5 mice) were in direct contact with OVA-specific T cells, few RelBlo BCL6+ B cells were in contact with cognate T cells (17%, n = 79) (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence histology data shown in Figure 7G and 7H.

claim: BCL6 expression was substantially increased in B cells in cell cultures provided with continuous stimulation of αCD40 and IL-4/21, however, BCL6+ cells remained RelB+ and IRF4+, resembling GC precursors.
source: BCL6 expression was substantially increased in B cells in cell cultures provided with continuous stimulation of αCD40 and IL-4/21, however, BCL6+ cells remained RelB+ and IRF4+, resembling GC precursors (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 8B and 8C.

claim: After a half-day deprivation of αCD40 and IL-4/21, a population of cells with substantially higher expression of BCL6 was generated.
source: After a half-day deprivation of αCD40 and IL-4/21, a population of cells with substantially higher expression of BCL6 was generated (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: BCL6hi cells generated after deprivation of αCD40 and IL-4/21 expressed low levels of RelB and IRF4, resembling GC B cells.
source: These BCL6hi cells expressed low levels of RelB and IRF4, resembling GC B cells (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Removal of either αCD40 or IL-4/21 alone was insufficient to allow robust generation of the GC-like population.
source: Notably, removal of either αCD40 or IL-4/21 alone was insufficient to allow robust generation of the GC-like population (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: BCL6hi RelBlo cells underwent several more rounds of cell division than BCL6int RelB+ cells in washout cultures.
source: In addition, cell division analysis of washout cultures indicated that BCL6hi RelBlo cells underwent several more rounds of cell division than BCL6int RelB+ cells (Figure 8E), suggesting that BCL6hi cells differentiated from BCL6int RelB+ precursors that have undergone at least one further division without T cell-associated stimuli (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is supported by CFSE dilution data from in vitro cultures shown in Figure 8E.

claim: GC B cell precursors (BCL6int RelB+ IRF4+) expressed much higher levels of bcl6 mRNA than that of BCL6lo RelBlo IRF4lo cells of washout cultures.
source: Consistent with this, GC B cell precursors (BCL6int RelB+ IRF4+) expressed much higher levels of bcl6 mRNA than that of BCL6lo RelBlo IRF4lo cells of washout cultures (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PrimeFlow RNA assay data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: BCL6hi GC B cells evidenced a significantly greater increase of BCL6 protein than that of bcl6 mRNA, suggesting both transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of BCL6 expression occurs during the transition to the BCL6hi GC B cell state.
source: Notably however, BCL6hi GC B cells evidenced a significantly greater increase of BCL6 protein than that of bcl6 mRNA, suggesting both transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of BCL6 expression occurs during the transition to the BCL6hi GC B cell state (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by PrimeFlow RNA assay data comparing protein and mRNA levels shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Only the YFPhi population gives rise to BCL6hi IRF4lo RelBlo cells, but the YFPlo population does not.
source: Although the shortened initial culture with αCD40 and IL-4/21 results in fewer BCL6hi RelB- IRF4- GC B cells, the results indicate that only the YFPhi population gives rise to BCL6hi IRF4lo RelBlo cells, but the YFPlo population does not (Figure 8—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell sorting and re-culture data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2C and 2D.

claim: CD40 signaling is clearly a necessary component of GC formation.
source: Although CD40 signaling is clearly a necessary component of GC formation, a transcriptional program consistent with persistent CD40 signaling is not seen in GC B cells (Basso et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Basso et al., 2004.

claim: Chronic CD40 signaling is known to antagonize GC B cell formation and instead promotes plasma cell differentiation.
source: Moreover, chronic CD40 signaling is known to antagonize GC B cell formation and instead promotes plasma cell differentiation (Allman et al., 1996; Bolduc et al., 2010; Kishi et al., 2010; Nutt et al., 2015; Saito et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Allman et al., 1996; Bolduc et al., 2010; Kishi et al., 2010; Nutt et al., 2015; Saito et al., 2007).

claim: IRF4 appears to be essential for the differentiation of both GC B cells and ASCs.
source: However, IRF4 appears to be essential for the differentiation of both GC B cells and ASCs (Klein et al., 2006; Ochiai et al., 2013; Sciammas et al., 2006; Willis et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (Klein et al., 2006; Ochiai et al., 2013; Sciammas et al., 2006; Willis et al., 2014).

claim: IL-21 has been shown to be an important regulator of both GC B cell and plasma cell differentiation in a B-cell intrinsic manner.
source: To further confound things, a key cytokine secreted by Tfh cells, IL-21, has also been shown to be an important regulator of both GC B cell and plasma cell differentiation in a B-cell intrinsic manner (Ozaki et al., 2004, Ozaki et al., 2002; Zotos et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Ozaki et al., 2004, Ozaki et al., 2002; Zotos et al., 2010).

claim: The transcriptional repressor BCL6 is essential for GC B cell development.
source: The transcriptional repressor BCL6 is essential for GC B cell development (De Silva and Klein, 2015; Dent et al., 1997; Huang et al., 2014; Kitano et al., 2011) and represses the transcription factors IRF4 and Blimp1, preventing ASC formation (Basso and Dalla-Favera, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple published studies (De Silva and Klein, 2015; Dent et al., 1997; Huang et al., 2014; Kitano et al., 2011; Basso and Dalla-Favera, 2012).

claim: High levels of IRF4 or induction of Blimp1 represses transcription of Bcl6 and facilitates ASC differentiation.
source: By contrast, high levels of IRF4 or induction of Blimp1 represses transcription of Bcl6 and facilitates ASC differentiation (Nutt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nutt et al., 2015.

claim: Bcl6 protein levels can be regulated at both the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels.
source: Bcl6 protein levels can be regulated at both the transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels (Duan et al., 2012; Saito et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Duan et al., 2012; Saito et al., 2006; Takahashi et al., 2012).

claim: CD40 signaling plays a pivotal role in the generation of GCs.
source: CD40 signaling plays a pivotal role in the generation of GCs (Foy et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Foy et al., 1996.

claim: Initial B cell commitment to the GC lineage and divergence from the short-term antibody secreting cell path occurs during the time period when responding B and T cells engage at the periphery of follicles.
source: Initial B cell commitment to the GC lineage and divergence from the short-term antibody secreting cell (ASC) path occurs during this time period (Kerfoot et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kerfoot et al., 2011.

claim: Intermediate levels of BCL6 have been observed in some activated B cells prior to follicular re-entry and GC seeding.
source: Intermediate levels of BCL6 have been observed in some activated B cells prior to follicular re-entry and GC seeding (Kerfoot et al., 2011; Kitano et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kerfoot et al., 2011; Kitano et al., 2011).

claim: Tfh migration into the follicle interior precedes that of GC committed B cells.
source: Interestingly, Tfh migration into the follicle interior precedes that of GC committed B cells (Kerfoot et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kerfoot et al., 2011.

claim: GC B cell differentiation is a two-stage process: a T-cell contact and CD40-dependent phase that generates RelB+ IRF4+ BCL6int GC precursors, and a phase immediately following that is prevented by further CD40 signaling but nevertheless needed to complete their transition to BCL6hi GC B cells.
source: We find that GC B cell differentiation is a two-stage process; (1) a T-cell contact and CD40-dependent phase that generates RelB+ IRF4+ BCL6int GC precursors and (2) a phase immediately following that is prevented by further CD40 signaling but nevertheless needed to complete their transition to BCL6hi GC B cells.
evidence: The claim is a synthesis of the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The transition of GC precursors to the Bcl6hi state is discouraged by Th-derived CD40L during the early stages of adaptive immune responses.
source: Together our results are consistent with the idea that the transition of GC precursors to the Bcl6hi state is discouraged by Th-derived CD40L during the early stages of adaptive immune responses.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: IRF4 is required for both ASC and GC development, although its sustained expression preferentially promotes ASC associated genes, subverting the GC pathway.
source: Notably, IRF4 is required for both ASC and GC development, although its sustained expression preferentially promotes ASC associated genes, subverting the GC pathway (Kwon et al., 2009; Ochiai et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Kwon et al., 2009; Ochiai et al., 2013).

claim: IRF4 is known to directly bind to and represses the Bcl6 promoter.
source: The requirement for prior IRF4 expression had come as a bit of a surprise since IRF4 is known to directly bind to and represses the Bcl6 promoter (Basso et al., 2010; Saito et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Basso et al., 2010; Saito et al., 2007).

claim: Within mature GCs, BCL6 controls B cell differentiation by regulating cell cycle genes and some terminal differentiation factors.
source: Within mature GCs, BCL6 controls B cell differentiation by regulating cell cycle genes and some terminal differentiation factors (Bunting and Melnick, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bunting and Melnick, 2013.

claim: Repressed BCL6 target genes in dark zone GC B cells include cd38, irf4 and prdm1.
source: Repressed BCL6 target genes in dark zone GC B cells include cd38, irf4 and prdm1, however precursor B cells displayed only a partial GC phenotype and have not yet fully suppressed surface expression of CD38.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of BCL6 target genes and observations from the manuscript.

claim: IL-21 is required for even intermediate Bcl6 levels in the in vitro culture system.
source: IL-21 is required for even intermediate Bcl6 levels in our in vitro culture system, and in vivo B cell expression of IL-21R is required for maximal BCL6 levels in GC B cells (Linterman et al., 2010; Zotos et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to published studies (Linterman et al., 2010; Zotos et al., 2010).

claim: Tfh cells are known to express CD40L transcripts at levels comparable to Th2 cells.
source: However, Tfh cells are known to express CD40L transcripts at levels comparable to Th2 cells (Nurieva et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nurieva et al., 2008.

claim: Exposure to IL-21 in the absence of anti-CD40 within the in vitro culture system leads to apoptosis without GC B cell formation.
source: Moreover, exposure to IL-21 in the absence of anti-CD40 within our in vitro culture system, even if there was prior CD40 ligation, leads to apoptosis without GC B cell formation, consistent with previous reports of IL-21 induced apoptosis (Spolski and Leonard, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to Spolski and Leonard, 2008.

claim: Higher affinity B cells with a greater capacity to acquire and present antigen to T cells preferentially formed plasmablasts during early adaptive immune responses.
source: This is consistent with prior studies demonstrating that higher affinity B cells with a greater capacity to acquire and present antigen to T cells preferentially formed plasmablasts during early adaptive immune responses (Schwickert et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schwickert et al., 2011.

claim: Particulate antigen has been reported to be inequitably distributed between daughters during cell division, such that a subset of B cells receive less antigen and have a reduced capacity to stimulate cognate T cells.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that particulate antigen has also been reported to be inequitably distributed between daughters during cell division, such that a subset of B cells receive less antigen and have a reduced capacity to stimulate cognate T cells (Thaunat et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thaunat et al., 2012.

claim: Persistent pathogen-derived antigen during chronic Salmonella infection results in large numbers of extrafollicular ASCs and impaired GC responses.
source: Similarly, persistent pathogen-derived antigen during chronic Salmonella infection results in large numbers of extrafollicular ASCs and impaired GC responses (Di Niro et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Di Niro et al., 2015.

claim: The introduction of additional Ag potentiates the magnitude of Tfh and GC cells when introduced at a later time point.
source: However our results contrast with a previous finding that the introduction of additional Ag potentiates the magnitude of Tfh and GC cells (Baumjohann et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baumjohann et al., 2013.

claim: Mature GCs harbor a distinct micro-anatomic compartment, the dark zone, that has a paucity of Tfh cells.
source: In this regard it is interesting to note that mature GCs harbor a distinct micro-anatomic compartment, the dark zone, that has a paucity of Tfh cells (Hauser et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hauser et al., 2010.

claim: An unequal distribution of BCL6 resulting from asymmetric cell division has previously been reported in a subset of germinal center B cells.
source: An unequal distribution of BCL6 resulting from asymmetric cell division has previously been reported in a subset of germinal center B cells (Barnett et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barnett et al., 2012.
